newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Analysts laud Taiwan bank reserve reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Analysts laud Taiwan bank reserve reform plan.

text.p: The central bank's plan to liberalise Taiwan's bank reserve system along international lines would benefit the market by facilitating transfers of banking system funds, analysts said on Thursday.
But the reform, approved in a board meeting on Thursday, would have no immediate impact because the central bank has yet to set dates for implementation, experts added.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told reporters after the meeting that the bank would gradually lower banks' reserve requirements "at the appropriate time" but gave no timetable.

"Obviously if the reform is pushed through it would improve the efficiency of monetary flow in the banking system, so it would be a step in the right direction," said George Hou, fund manager for Jardine Fleming.
"But the market already was anticipating the central bank's announcing the reform. The important thing, which the bank has not addressed, is how and when the reform would be launched."

The central bank currently sets range limits for banks' reserve requirements -- 15-40 percent for checking deposits, 10-35 percent for passbook deposits, five to 20 percent for saving deposits and seven to 25 percent for time deposits.
Under the liberalisation, the central bank would gradually scrap the limits and ultimately allow financial institutions to determine their own reserve levels, Sheu said.
The relaxation would amount to a cost-cutting measure for banks, analysts said.

"The fewer restrictions there are, the more banks can cut costs and put their money to immediate good use, allowing for more freedom in operation," said a dealer at a foreign bank who asked that his name not be used.
Jardine Fleming's Hou cautioned, however, that the central bank was wary of letting go too fast lest the reform destabilise the banking system.
"The bank is worried that if it allows the reserve level to go down too fast, there would be too much excess money in the system, creating chaos in the market," Hou said.

Showing that financial stability was a top priority, Sheu said on Thursday the central bank board had decided to maintain the current "stable-to-loose" monetary policy and leave reserve requirements unchanged.
Sheu said the bank would continue to conduct open-market operations to maintain balance in the monetary system.

The central bank has kept a similar monetary policy for weeks, trying to strike a balance that keeps interest rates low enough to stimulate the flagging economy without undermining the interests of bank depositors.
Sheu encouraged other government departments to work with the central bank in a concerted effort to stimulate investment, saying the bank could not do this alone.
"The current slow economy is not something that can be solved solely by central bank monetary policy," Sheu said. "We need the cooperation of other agencies in order to boost investment incentive."
The bank also decided on Thursday not to adjust its target range for M2 money supply growth for 1996, keeping the current zone of 9-14 percent.

M2 growth rose to a year-on-year 8.69 percent in September from 8.44 percent in August but bank officials have said 1996 full-year M2 growth was unlikely to reach the target, spurring speculation that a downward revision might be in the works.
